{{No footnotes|date=December 2023}}
In [[algebra]], the '''nilradical''' of a [[Lie algebra]] is a nilpotent [[Ideal (Lie algebra)|ideal]], which is as large as possible. 

The nilradical <math>\mathfrak{nil}(\mathfrak g)</math> of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is its maximal [[nilpotent ideal]], which exists because the sum of any two nilpotent ideals is nilpotent. It is an ideal in the [[radical of a Lie algebra|radical]] <math>\mathfrak{rad}(\mathfrak{g})</math> of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. The quotient of a Lie algebra by its nilradical is a [[reductive Lie algebra|reductive]] Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{red}}</math>. However, the corresponding [[short exact sequence]]
:<math> 0 \to \mathfrak{nil}(\mathfrak g)\to \mathfrak g\to \mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{red}}\to 0</math>
does not split in general (i.e., there isn't always a ''subalgebra'' complementary to <math>\mathfrak{nil}(\mathfrak g)</math> in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>). This is in contrast to the [[Levi decomposition]]: the short exact sequence
:<math> 0 \to \mathfrak{rad}(\mathfrak g)\to \mathfrak g\to \mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{ss}}\to 0</math>
does split (essentially because the quotient <math>\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{ss}}</math> is semisimple).
